title: Teaching About Race and Racism in Schools
abstract: There has been considerable debate among educators, policymakers, and the broader public regarding whether and how to include discussions of race and racism in school curricula. Some argue that teaching about race and the experience of racially marginalized groups can reinforce racial divisions, whereas others contend that it fosters understanding, reflects historical and contemporary reality, and improves student outcomes. In this paper, we briefly review the political landscape of this debate, detailing both the backlash and support for formally incorporating lessons about race and racism into school curricula. We review the empirical literature on the benefits and challenges of this instruction and offer recommendations for how educators and students can effectively engage with race and racism in the classroom. We recommend that school curricula on race and racism offer insight into both racialized identities and processes of racialization and that they address racism at both the individual and the structural levels. Adopting these recommendations would provide students with the building blocks for understanding how race and racism manifest and why they matter to civic life without putting undue pressure or emphasis on any one category, student, or institution.
